facts.fact: The canary evaluator verdict was FAIL. The candidate had 4 errors in 24 requests (16.67% error rate). The stable baseline had 0 errors in 24 requests. The maximum permitted error rate is 2%.
Three thresholds were breached: absolute error rate, error-rate delta against stable, and error-budget burn rate (166.7x against a 14.4x limit).
Latency was not the problem. The candidate p95 was 7.22 ms against a 300 ms limit. The Mann-Whitney test was not significant (p=0.0949). The health endpoint was OK.

The commit under investigation, 0a4020ec, changed calculate_discount in app/app/routes/orders.py. It removed the `customer_tier.strip().lower()` normalisation and the `.get(..., 0.0)` default for unknown tiers. It replaced them with a direct `TIER_RATES[customer_tier]` lookup. The removed docstring said tier names arrive from many clients in any casing and unknown tiers get no discount.
At the broken commit, calculate_discount does `round(subtotal * TIER_RATES[customer_tier], 2)`. TIER_RATES has only the lowercase keys 'standard', 'premium' and 'enterprise'.

create_order passes the client-supplied order.customer_tier straight to calculate_discount. There is no validation, no normalisation and no exception handling around the call. The only declared constraint on customer_tier is a free-form string with default 'standard'.
The revision log records an HTTP 500 on a POST /api/v1/orders probe, with an error reported inside calculate_discount.

The revision log is inconsistent with the code. It reports a ZeroDivisionError at orders.py line 34, and its timestamps are from 2026-10-19, while the evaluation ran on 2026-10-27. At the broken commit, line 34 is `ORDERS_DB = {}`. calculate_discount contains no division, and it spans lines 44-46.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The 4 failed canary requests used a customer_tier value that is not an exact lowercase key of TIER_RATES. Examples are 'Premium', 'ENTERPRISE', ' premium ' or an unknown tier. The direct lookup raised KeyError, which FastAPI returned as HTTP 500. The old code handled these inputs by normalising and defaulting to a 0.0 rate.
hypotheses.rationale: The diff removes exactly this handling, the docstring documents the mixed-casing input, and the failures are confined to the candidate while stable (old code) had 0 errors. The 4/24 error rate fits a minority of probe requests with non-canonical tiers. The Python code makes the KeyError path unambiguous for such input.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The error text in revision_logs (ZeroDivisionError, line 34) does not describe the real failure mechanism. It may be stale, from a different revision, or a synthetic or templated entry. The real exception is probably KeyError.
hypotheses.rationale: The log timestamps predate this run. The reported exception type and line number do not match the code at 0a4020ec.

hypotheses.hypothesis: No other part of the diff contributes to the regression.
hypotheses.rationale: The diff touches only calculate_discount. The latency data shows no significant shift.

suspected_change.reason: The refactor replaced the normalising, defaulting lookup `TIER_RATES.get(customer_tier.strip().lower(), 0.0)` with `TIER_RATES[customer_tier]`. Any tier that is not an exact lowercase key now raises an unhandled KeyError, which becomes an HTTP 500.

proposed_fix_summary: Restore the previous behaviour in calculate_discount in app/app/routes/orders.py. Look up `TIER_RATES.get(customer_tier.strip().lower(), 0.0)`, so tier names are case-insensitive and whitespace-tolerant, and unknown tiers get a 0.0 discount. Keep the docstring that documents this contract. This is a minimal revert of the lookup logic and leaves the rest of the commit untouched. Add a regression test that calls calculate_discount with 'Premium', 'ENTERPRISE', ' premium ' and an unknown tier such as 'gold'. It should assert discounts of 10%, 20%, 10% and 0% respectively. On the broken commit these raise KeyError, which the test should catch and report as an AssertionError. On the fixed code they pass.
